WHAT IS AN ADVISORY OPINION? An advisory opinion is a legal interpretation of the Rhode Island Code of Ethics issued by the Ethics Commission which provides specific guidance about a particular and impending circumstance. Advisory opinions are based upon the representations made by, or on behalf of, the persons or entities requesting them, and are not the result of adversarial or investigative proceedings.

WHO CAN REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? A person subject to the Code of Ethics may request an advisory opinion about a particular provision of the Code which may affect him or her. WHEN SHOULD I REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? If you believe you may face a real or potential conflict of interest, the time to request an advisory opinion is before you take any official action.

HOW DO I REQUEST AN ADVISORY OPINION? To request an advisory opinion, you must either mail or hand-deliver to the Commission a letter containing your original signature and the following information: • Your name, official position, and a description of your duties; • Your daytime telephone number and e-mail address; • Briefly, the name, jurisdiction and powers of your agency, commission, or office; • The nature of the potential conflict; • A summary of relevant facts; and • Any time constraints.

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER I SUBMIT MY REQUEST? ► Letter confirming receipt ► Draft recommendation prepared by staff attorney ► You are strongly encouraged to attend hearing ► Affirmative vote of 5 of 9 Commissioners required ► You will receive written copy ► Also available on Ethics Commission website ► Advisory Opinion and request are public records

Who is required to file? ► All state and municipal elected officials ► Candidates for state or municipal elected office ► All state and some municipal appointed officials ► Some public employees who hold major decision- making positions
All officials required to file must continue to file Financial Disclosure Statements until they have been out of office for one full calendar year.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-02
November 19, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION
(Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting)
Extends deadline for course withdrawals without extenuating circumstances
Approved by FSEC 10/28/26 (as amended)
Legislation effective starting Fall 2027
Rationale: URI’s current policy for course withdrawals allows students to withdraw from a course by week six into the semester. At the end of week six, they need to have extenuating circumstances with supporting documentation for approval of a late drop. Many - most - courses do not post midterm grades by week six, however, making students predict their success in the course before they have any real data. Students either drop the course for fear of not doing well and miss the chance to succeed or stay in and try and succeed when they should have dropped it. When students ask for a W too late, without extenuating circumstances, their late drop petition gets denied even if their reasoning is sound.

For regular session classes, the revised version of this legislation would extend the “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadline for undergraduate students from six weeks to nine weeks. Graduate students would continue to have the existing deadline of six weeks.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments.
1. Moved the “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadline from 11 weeks (originally proposed) to nine weeks. Although five of the ten comparable institutions surveyed (see below) have “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” deadlines at 11 weeks, there was concern about making such a substantial change.

2. Maintained the current ‘Drop through Ecampus’ option for students between the fourth and sixth weeks in the regular semester. The original legislation eliminated the ability of students to drop classes through Ecampus after the three-week add period. The revised legislation does not change the existing ‘Drop through Ecampus’ option for weeks 4-6. As a result, there should be minimal/no change in the total number of withdrawal forms processed.
3. Removed faculty signatures on “Withdraw without extenuating circumstances” forms submitted between the sixth and ninth weeks. Faculty signatures are currently required for withdrawals after the sixth week of classes. To reduce administrative burden, faculty signatures would no longer be required for withdrawals occurring before the end of the ninth week. As per current practice, faculty signatures would still be required for withdrawal requests submitted after the ninth week of classes.

4. Restricted the legislation to undergraduate students. The current withdrawal policy applies to both graduate and undergraduate students. The Graduate School has requested that graduate students retain the six-week ‘withdraw without extenuating circumstances’ deadline.
DATA
Ten comparable universities were reviewed: half allow late drops without extenuating circumstances until the eleventh week of the regular semester, and all have a later date than URI and the same withdrawal date for graduate and undergraduate students.
*See “Addendum to Proposal Change to URI’s Late Withdrawal of a Course Policy” document to review the comparable universities and their full policies

Potential impacts: This proposal has been vetted by ESAC (Enrollment Services Advisory Committee), a URI internal administrative body that includes academic deans or representatives from each degree-granting college and the directors of student-supporting service offices. To ensure that undergraduate students understand the academic and/or financial implications of a ‘W’, ESAC recommended that course withdrawal forms remain required between the end of the six-week ‘Drop in ECampus’ period and the last day of classes. Each form must be signed by an academic affairs advisor/dean of the college in which the student is enrolled before being processed by enrollment services.
This proposal should not change the number of withdrawal forms being processed, and the per-form processing time for undergraduate withdrawal forms submitted between weeks 6-9 will be reduced significantly because students no longer need to provide extenuating circumstances. There will be fewer meetings and less work required for undergraduate students to document extenuating circumstances.

This change will also greatly benefit staff working in areas such as Health Services, Student Support & Advocacy Services, and Disability, Access, & Inclusion. Over the past four Fall semesters (see below), an average of 1,379 “Withdraw with extenuating circumstances” requests were processed each semester. Each of these requests required someone at the university to certify them as such, a process that takes a substantial amount of time each semester. The new policy would reduce the average number of “Withdraw with extenuating circumstances” requests from 1,379 to 847 per semester, a ~40% decrease.

ORIGINAL 8.34.10 Dropping a Course. A course may be dropped by official procedures determined by the Office of Enrollment Services (e-campus) on or before the end of the third week of classes (Drop Period) with no mark on a student’s transcript. Courses may be dropped through e-campus between the fourth and the end of the sixth week of classes (Withdrawal Period) and will be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” After the end of the sixth week (Late Withdrawal Period), a student may drop a course only in exceptional circumstances and only with authorization of the dean of the college in which the student is enrolled. Such drops will also be recognized on a student’s transcript with a “W.” If the student has not dropped a course by the end of the withdrawal period the instructor must submit a grade. All requests to drop courses after the end of the Late Withdrawal Period must be requested/approved by the student’s academic dean by the last day of classes for the term in which the drop is sought. Only in exceptional circumstances and with significant supporting documentation will exceptions to this deadline be considered. Failure or low grades on assignments/exams or lack of attendance do not constitute exceptional circumstances. Fees will not be adjusted downward for courses dropped after the end of the “add” period (see 8.43.20 for adjustment of fees). #10-11—23, #12-13–24, #21-22-6

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-03 November 19, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting Creation of a College Liaison Special Committee (one semester trial) Approved by FSEC 11/04/26 Effective Date: Start of spring semester 2027 The College Liaison Special Committee (CLSC) shall consist of up to ten senators, one from each college that elects Faculty Senators and one from the Library (henceforth referred to as ‘units’) , who are referred to as the ‘Liaison’ from their unit to the Faculty Senate.
If the Faculty Senate votes to approve creation of this Special Committee in fall 2026 , Senate Staff will contact senators from each unit and solicit volunteer(s) from among their number to serve as the Liaison from that unit during the spring 2027 semester .
If there are multiple volunteers from a given unit, senators from that unit will vote to elect one liaison from among their senators volunteering for the role.
CLSC membership will be confirmed by Faculty Senate vote prior to its beginning work.
The CLSC will be chaired by the Vice President of the Faculty Senate, who serves as a non-voting member.

CLSC members are charged with ensuring that faculty in each college are informed of pertinent university-level matters and communicate senate- and college-level concerns in both directions.
Liaisons attend all-college faculty meetings and will be given the opportunity to give a report on senate activities.
Liaisons also attend meetings of the Faculty Senate in their role as a current senator.
Liaisons will have two responsibilities in addition to attending college- and senate-level meetings.
First, Liaisons provide a monthly written update regarding senate/university-level matters to faculty in their college.
Second, Liaisons represent their college at meetings of the CLSC.
The committee will meet at least once per semester to address issues requiring inter-college coordination.
These may include, but are not limited to, best practices in college-level faculty governance and fostering inter-college research or academic collaborations.
Liaisons are encouraged to submit topics for discussion at CLSC meetings to the Faculty Senate Vice President, who will compile them into a meeting agenda.

The CLSC can vote to refer a matter to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for additional consideration and possible action by the full Senate.
At the end of the spring 2027 semester, the Senate Vice President will give a report to the Faculty Senate listing all matters referred by the CLSC during the previous semester and their current status.
At that time, the CLSC may choose to submit legislation requesting Faculty Senate authorization to continue as a Special Committee in the 2027-28 academic year.
If the CLSC does not receive an affirmative reauthorization vote from the Faculty Senate in spring 2027, it shall be dissolved.
